strengths: GEPA is a clear and meaningful contribution: it combines trajectory-level natural-language reflection, module-wise prompt mutation, and instance-wise Pareto candidate selection into a coherent optimizer for compound LLM systems.

The empirical gains are substantial and consistent. GEPA outperforms MIPROv2 across four benchmarks and two model families, and it substantially exceeds the reported GRPO results for Qwen3-8B while using fewer system rollouts.

The evaluation covers diverse settings—multi-hop QA, retrieval, instruction following, and privacy-aware delegation—rather than relying on a single benchmark. Held-out test sets are used, including an out-of-distribution IFBench test set.
The comparison with a strong prompt-optimization baseline uses approximately matched rollout budgets, and the paper provides learning curves rather than only final scores.

The Pareto-selection ablation supports an important design choice, with sizable improvements over always selecting the globally best candidate. The paper also analyzes prompt length and reports encouraging, though preliminary, code-optimization results.
The method and motivation are presented clearly, with pseudocode, the reflection meta-prompt, optimization trajectories, and final prompts included in the appendices.
weaknesses: The experiments appear to report single stochastic optimization runs despite nonzero sampling temperatures. There are no confidence intervals, seed-level results, or significance tests, making it difficult to assess the stability of the gains and of the sometimes large differences between GEPA and GEPA+Merge.

The central causal claim about natural-language reflection is not adequately ablated. The paper does not compare against mutations without textual feedback, score-only reflection, alternative feedback formulations, or simpler iterative prompt-revision methods. Consequently, the contribution of reflection relative to search and repeated validation is unclear.

GEPA uses per-instance validation scores to construct and repeatedly sample from its Pareto frontier. This is substantially richer validation-set access than ordinary aggregate early stopping and may differ from the information available to the baselines. Although held-out test results remain meaningful, the fairness and practical interpretation of the optimizer comparison require further analysis.

Rollout count alone is an incomplete cost measure. GEPA additionally invokes an LLM to reflect and synthesize prompts, while GRPO incurs backward-pass training costs; proposal-token usage, monetary cost, wall-clock time, and total compute are not reported. Thus, claims about computational efficiency beyond environment-rollout efficiency are insufficiently supported.

The empirical baseline set is narrow for establishing the source-of-improvement and state-of-the-art claims: only MIPROv2 represents prompt optimization, with no direct experiments against reflection/textual-gradient or other evolutionary prompt optimizers discussed in related work.

The GRPO comparison is limited to one 8B model, LoRA adaptation, and a modest manual hyperparameter search. This is useful evidence but does not support a broad conclusion that reflective prompt evolution generally outperforms reinforcement learning.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no implementation or artifact release is identified, and important details such as random seeds, number of independent runs, optimizer-model accounting, and end-to-end resource consumption are absent. The inference-time code experiments are also explicitly preliminary and use only 35 KernelBench tasks.

strengths: GEPA is a clear and practically relevant method that combines trajectory-level natural-language feedback, reflective prompt mutation, and instance-wise Pareto candidate selection.
The main evaluation covers four meaningfully different tasks, modular systems with multiple prompts, and both an open-weight model and a commercial model.

Reported improvements over the unoptimized systems and MIPROv2 are large and consistent across the eight task/model combinations, with held-out test evaluation and approximately matched system-rollout budgets.
The manuscript provides understandable pseudocode, the reflection meta-prompt, search trajectories, learning curves, and final optimized prompts.
The preliminary kernel-optimization results suggest that the method may extend beyond conventional language benchmarks.
weaknesses: The experiments do not isolate the central source of improvement. There is no ablation removing textual feedback, replacing reflection with generic prompt mutation, or using scalar feedback alone. Consequently, the respective contributions of richer supervision, reflection, and evolutionary search remain unclear.

The baseline coverage is inadequate for the main methodological claim. TextGrad and other reflection-, feedback-, or evolutionary-prompt optimizers are discussed but not evaluated; MIPROv2 is the only substantial prompt-optimization baseline.

Results appear to come from single stochastic runs, with no error bars, confidence intervals, significance tests, or sensitivity analysis. This is especially concerning given stochastic generation, small test sets of approximately 221–300 examples, and several claimed improvements of only a few percentage points.

The comparison with GRPO is not controlled for total computation, generated tokens, wall-clock time, optimizer-model calls, or tuning effort. It is limited to Qwen3-8B with LoRA, and GRPO underperforms the untuned baseline on two tasks, raising concern about baseline strength. The headline claim about outperforming reinforcement learning is therefore too broad.

GEPA receives hand-designed, task-specific evaluator feedback that can reveal gold documents, failed constraints, or metric decompositions, whereas GRPO consumes scalar rewards. Rollout counts consequently compare samples with substantially different information content and do not by themselves establish superior learning efficiency.

Reproducibility details are incomplete: the model and decoding configuration used for reflection are unclear, non-rollout optimizer calls are not accounted for, random seeds and exact sampled splits are absent, and no executable artifact is provided in the manuscript.

The method repeatedly evaluates candidates on every validation instance and uses per-instance validation scores for search. This validation-intensive procedure weakens the practical sample-efficiency narrative and may overfit the validation set, despite the reported test results.

The code-optimization study is explicitly preliminary, uses only 35 KernelBench tasks, and lacks matched-budget comparisons and repeated trials; it does not yet support broader inference-time-search claims.

strengths: GEPA is a clear and practically meaningful contribution: it combines trajectory-level natural-language reflection, evolutionary prompt mutation, and instance-wise Pareto selection for optimizing multi-module LLM systems.

The empirical gains are substantial. Across four tasks and two model families, GEPA consistently improves over the unoptimized systems and MIPROv2, with especially strong results on HotpotQA and PUPA.

The paper provides compelling evidence of rollout efficiency relative to the evaluated GRPO setup, including performance-versus-budget curves and separate accounting of training versus validation rollouts.
The evaluation spans reasoning, retrieval, instruction following, and privacy-aware delegation, and uses held-out test sets. The out-of-distribution IFBench setup is particularly valuable.

The presentation is unusually transparent for a prompt-optimization paper: the algorithm, reflection meta-prompt, search trees, intermediate prompts, final prompts, rollout counts, and prompt-length analysis are extensively documented.
The Pareto-selection comparison provides useful evidence that candidate selection matters, while the inference-time kernel experiments suggest broader applicability beyond conventional prompt tuning.
weaknesses: The results appear to come from single stochastic optimization runs, despite nonzero sampling temperatures and random candidate/minibatch selection. No repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, or significance tests are reported, so robustness—particularly for modest differences—is unclear.

The ablation study does not isolate several central ingredients. There is no controlled removal of textual feedback, comparison against mutation without reflection, scalar-reward-only reflection, or a standard evolutionary baseline. Consequently, the gains cannot be cleanly attributed to the paper's principal claim about rich language feedback.

The comparison with GRPO is narrower than the title and framing suggest: it uses one 8B model, LoRA rather than full-parameter training, manually explored but incompletely characterized hyperparameters, and an implementation cited as a manuscript in preparation. GEPA also receives richer evaluator feedback than GRPO, so this establishes that this particular reflective optimizer can outperform this particular RL setup, not a broad superiority over reinforcement learning.

Rollout count is an informative but incomplete efficiency measure. GEPA incurs additional reflection/proposal-model calls and repeatedly evaluates a validation set, while methods produce prompts of different lengths. End-to-end token usage, wall-clock time, monetary cost, and compute would make the efficiency comparison substantially stronger.

Some important implementation details are underspecified, including the exact model and decoding configuration used for reflective prompt updates, random seeds, and complete optimizer-level costs. No explicit code or artifact release is identified, limiting reproducibility.

The use of per-instance validation scores to construct and repeatedly query the Pareto frontier creates a substantial adaptive validation-selection channel. Although final test sets remain held out, robustness to Pareto-set size and repeated validation reuse is not studied.

The preliminary kernel experiments are interesting but insufficiently controlled: they use small or early benchmark subsets and do not report repeated trials or fully matched compute budgets. They should be treated as exploratory rather than strong evidence of general inference-time-search effectiveness.

strengths: GEPA offers a clear and practically meaningful combination of trajectory-level natural-language reflection, evolutionary prompt mutation, and instance-wise Pareto candidate selection for optimizing compound LLM systems.

The empirical study is unusually broad: six downstream benchmarks, open and proprietary models, multiple strong prompt-optimization baselines, GRPO with both LoRA and full-parameter variants, cross-model transfer, and preliminary code-optimization applications.

The reported gains are substantial and mostly consistent. GEPA outperforms MIPROv2 across the main model/task combinations and generally surpasses 24,000-rollout GRPO runs with substantially fewer system rollouts.
The candidate-selection comparison against greedy selection and beam search provides useful evidence that the Pareto mechanism contributes materially beyond the common reflective-update harness.

The algorithm, optimization budgets, data splits, prompts, GRPO hyperparameters, costs, rollout curves, and optimized-prompt examples are documented extensively, supporting implementation and qualitative inspection.
The work has strong practical relevance for settings where model weights are inaccessible or system rollouts are expensive; the cross-model transfer result is particularly encouraging.
weaknesses: The main experiments appear to use only one optimization run per condition and report no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Prompt evolution, stochastic decoding, and GRPO are all high-variance procedures, so several modest differences—especially on IFBench, AIME, and LiveBench—cannot be assessed reliably.

The central comparison to GRPO is not fully controlled. GEPA receives rich textual and sometimes module-specific feedback, including failed constraints, missing gold documents, or evaluator traces, whereas GRPO is trained from scalar rewards. Counting only rollouts also omits reflection-model calls and substantial differences in training compute, making the broad claim that reflective prompt evolution outperforms RL stronger than the evidence supports.

There is no direct ablation isolating the paper's central reflection claim: performance with textual feedback should be compared against scalar-only reflection, generic self-reflection, no reflection, and global versus module-specific feedback. The existing ablation mainly establishes the value of Pareto selection.

GEPA repeatedly accesses per-instance validation scores to construct its Pareto frontier and to choose future mutation parents. This is a stronger and more adaptive use of validation labels than aggregate checkpoint selection, and it is not obviously matched by all baselines. A separate untouched development set or a study of validation-set overfitting is needed.

The method combines established ingredients—LLM-based prompt rewriting, textual feedback, evolutionary search, and quality-diversity/Pareto selection—so its conceptual novelty is primarily in the integration and empirical execution rather than a fundamentally new learning principle.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the extensive appendix: exact random seeds and repeated-run protocol are absent, the role/configuration of the reflection model is not stated with sufficient precision, and the manuscript's code-release link is blank in the reviewed version.

The inference-time kernel and adversarial-search studies are interesting but preliminary, use small task sets, and lack repeated trials and sufficiently matched search baselines; they should not carry much weight for the primary claims.

strengths: GEPA is an intuitive and practically relevant combination of trajectory-level natural-language reflection, evolutionary prompt mutation, and instance-wise Pareto candidate selection.

The evaluation spans six tasks, compound and single-module systems, open and proprietary models, and held-out train/validation/test splits. Reported gains over MIPROv2, TextGrad, Trace, and GRPO are often substantial.
The candidate-selection comparison provides useful evidence that the Pareto strategy can outperform greedy and beam-search alternatives under the authors' setup.
Cross-model prompt transfer is a compelling result, and the paper provides extensive implementation details, prompts, rollout curves, cost estimates, and optimizer configurations.
weaknesses: The central empirical results appear to come from single optimization runs, despite stochastic decoding, minibatch sampling, candidate selection, and small test sets. There are no confidence intervals, error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests. Repeating each of 30 AIME questions five times does not provide 150 independent test examples. Consequently, many claimed margins—especially differences of only a few points—cannot be distinguished from optimization or evaluation variance.

The headline comparison with GRPO is not sufficiently controlled. GEPA receives rich evaluator traces, including failed constraints and identities of missing gold documents, whereas GRPO receives scalar rewards. Reflection/proposal-model calls, their token costs, and the extra information in textual feedback are not normalized in the rollout comparison. The experiments therefore show that this supervision-rich prompt-search pipeline can use fewer task executions than one GRPO configuration, not that reflective prompt evolution is intrinsically more sample-efficient than reinforcement learning.

The GRPO evidence is too narrow for the paper's title and broad claims. Most comparisons use a single LoRA recipe, with only manually explored hyperparameters; full-parameter tuning is examined on only one simplified HoVer system and is presented mainly as a curve without repeated trials or a comprehensive table. Stronger or better-tuned RL baselines and compute-matched comparisons are needed.

The novelty is moderate: language-model reflection, textual-feedback optimization, evolutionary prompt search, and quality-diversity/Pareto search are all established ideas. The paper combines them effectively, but does not isolate the contribution of each major ingredient. In particular, it lacks ablations for textual versus scalar feedback, module-specific versus global feedback, reflection versus generic prompt proposal, reflection-model choice, and equal-token or equal-cost budgets.

Model selection and sample-efficiency reporting are ambiguous. The algorithm selects by validation performance, but the discussion repeatedly reports the number of rollouts needed to reach 'optimal test performance.' If these points are identified retrospectively from test curves, they are not legitimate stopping points and overstate practical sample efficiency.

The Merge component is unstable: it substantially helps some GPT-4.1 Mini settings but sharply degrades several Qwen results, including IFBench. The explanation is post hoc, and no validation-based policy for deciding when to merge is supplied.

The inference-time code and adversarial-search studies are preliminary and weakly controlled. Code search deliberately places the same tasks in the optimization and Pareto sets, comparisons do not clearly equalize total generations, retrieval, reflection calls, or compute, and results are given on small task subsets. The adversarial result largely exposes a literal output-format failure rather than demonstrating broad robustness analysis.

Aggregate scores average heterogeneous benchmark metrics without uncertainty or justification, potentially obscuring failures on individual tasks. Overall, the promising method is not supported by sufficiently rigorous, compute-fair, and statistically reliable evidence for its strongest claims.

strengths: The paper presents a clear, timely contribution: using natural-language execution and evaluation traces for reflective prompt evolution, combined with instance-level Pareto selection to preserve diverse candidate strategies.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad for prompt optimization, covering six tasks, single- and multi-module systems, open and proprietary models, and several strong baselines including MIPROv2, TextGrad, Trace, and GRPO.

The main results are compelling and practically meaningful. GEPA consistently improves over the unoptimized systems and leading prompt optimizers, while substantially outperforming GRPO on five of six Qwen3-8B tasks with far fewer environment rollouts.

The candidate-selection ablation provides concrete support for an important design choice: Pareto-based selection substantially outperforms greedy and beam-search alternatives across four tasks under a common harness.

Cross-model transfer from Qwen3-8B-optimized prompts to GPT-4.1 Mini is a valuable result, suggesting that GEPA learns reusable task instructions rather than merely exploiting model-specific behavior.

The paper provides useful practical evidence, including rollout-performance curves, prompt-length comparisons, cost information, full optimized prompts, search-tree visualizations, and an additional full-parameter GRPO comparison.

The method applies naturally to compound AI systems and closed-source models without weight updates, giving it substantial practical relevance. The preliminary kernel-generation results further indicate promising applicability beyond standard NLP benchmarks.
weaknesses: The experiments appear to report single optimization runs without confidence intervals, multiple random seeds, or significance tests. This is important because candidate evolution, model sampling, and relatively small test sets can all introduce substantial variance.

The sample-efficiency comparison counts environment rollouts but does not fully account for reflection-model calls, generated tokens, wall-clock time, or total compute. Consequently, the claim of being more efficient than reinforcement learning is well supported in rollout efficiency but not yet in overall computational efficiency.

The broad framing that prompt evolution can outperform reinforcement learning rests primarily on one RL method and one 8B model. GRPO also degrades below the baseline on IFBench, and GEPA trails it on AIME-2025, so the title and some general claims should be qualified.

Important reproducibility details are underspecified, particularly the precise reflection-model configuration, complete random-seed policy, the range and selection procedure for manually explored GRPO hyperparameters, and several task-specific GEPA settings.

The ablations do not fully isolate the value of each learning signal. Comparisons using scalar-only feedback, generic textual feedback, or reflection without task-specific evaluation traces would clarify how much improvement comes from rich feedback versus evolutionary search itself.

GEPA+Merge is inconsistent, substantially hurting Qwen3-8B performance on some tasks. The paper acknowledges this, but the method currently lacks a reliable criterion for allocating budget to crossover.

The inference-time code-search and adversarial-prompt experiments are interesting but preliminary, with limited task counts and baseline coverage; they should be interpreted as demonstrations rather than established general findings.
